analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to provide paid vacation leave, earned at 1 hour per 25 worked.
analysis.headline: The bill would give nearly all U.S. workers up to 80 hours of paid vacation a year, but since its July 2025 introduction it has received no hearing, no markup, and no vote, with all 86 cosponsors being Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require employers with even one worker to provide paid annual leave: 1 hour earned for every 25 hours worked, up to 80 hours (about two weeks) per year, starting from the first day on the job. Workers could use the leave for any reason without disclosing why, could not be penalized or counted absent for taking it, and would be paid out for unused leave when they leave a job. It is sitting in five House committees with no action scheduled.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who lack paid vacation — disproportionately low-wage, part-time, and tipped employees — gain a guaranteed minimum of up to two weeks of paid leave a year, accrued from day one, usable for any reason, with protections against retaliation, denial notices with a required alternative date, no requirement to find their own shift coverage, 40 hours of carryover, and payout of unused leave at separation at the higher of their recent average or final pay rate. Tipped workers must be paid at least the full applicable minimum wage while on leave. Workers already covered by stronger state laws or union contracts keep those rights [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal right to paid annual leave for virtually all employees: 1 hour accrued per 25 hours worked, up to 80 hours in any 12-month period, beginning at the start of employment
Lets workers use the leave for any reason, bars employers from demanding to know why, and caps required advance notice at two weeks (none at all for unforeseeable needs)
Protects workers from retaliation: employers may not fire, demote, cut hours, discipline, or count the leave under a no-fault attendance policy because someone took it
Requires employers to pay out unused leave at separation at the higher of the employee's three-year average rate or final rate, and to reinstate leave balances for workers rehired within 12 months
Guarantees tipped employees at least the applicable federal, state, or local minimum wage while on leave, rather than the lower tipped base rate
Provides private enforcement with attorney's fees, a class-action option, and a two-to-three-year statute of limitations, plus Labor Department investigation and subpoena authority
Preserves stronger state and local leave laws and union contracts, and lets union members enforce bargained leave provisions through grievance and arbitration

analysis.who_pays: Employers bear the direct cost: up to 80 hours of wages per employee per year (more if they offer it voluntarily), plus recordkeeping, written policies, leave-balance tracking, and paid-out leave at separation. The bill has no small-business exemption — a covered employer is any employer with even one employee — and economists generally expect some of the cost to reach consumers through prices or to show up as slower hiring. Federal, state, and congressional employers, including congressional offices under the Congressional Accountability Act, also must comply [S2].

drawbacks.text: Up to 80 hours of paid leave per employee per year is a direct payroll cost for every covered employer, and the bill covers employers with as few as one employee, so small businesses with thin margins absorb the mandate with no phase-in beyond a 180-day effective date
Tipped workers are guaranteed only the minimum wage during leave — not their usual take-home pay with tips — so their paycheck while on leave can be well below a normal week

The bill lets employers deny specific leave requests for a 'bona fide business reason' with an alternative date within 30 days, which gives scheduling power to the employer and could make guaranteed leave hard to actually use in industries with rigid scheduling

The 80-hour annual cap and 40-hour carryover limit are modest compared with paid-leave guarantees in other wealthy countries, and the mandate replaces vacation only — sick leave, family leave, and holidays are explicitly excluded and separately governed

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the guarantee of paid time off — earned from day one, usable for any reason, with real anti-retaliation teeth and payout at separation — is a substantial, tangible benefit, especially for the low-wage and part-time workers least likely to have any paid vacation today. The costs fall on employers and, in part, on consumers, and the bill already includes business accommodations (a 2-week notice limit, employer denial rights for bona fide business reasons, an 80-hour cap, and collective bargaining agreement transition timing) that soften the burden while also trimming the benefit. The main honest objection is the absence of any small-business exemption or phase-in; the counterweight is that employers may already loan leave and the accrual rate means the cost tracks hours actually worked.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to five House committees on the day it was introduced, and none of them has held a hearing, marked it up, or sent it to the floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Seth Magaziner introduced the Protected Time Off Act on July 25, 2025, joined by dozens of original Democratic cosponsors
A total of 86 House Democrats had signed on as cosponsors

The same day, the House referred the bill to five committees — Education and Workforce, House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, Judiciary, and Transportation and Infrastructure — a multi-committee referral that means several chairs would each have to act
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action appears in the record after the referral
The 119th Congress runs through January 3, 2027, so the bill technically remains alive but has no scheduled action

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, employers are better off: no mandate has taken effect and none is on a path to a vote, while workers without paid leave remain without one.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers avoiding a leave mandate, so far

sides.party_line_note: All 86 cosponsors are House Democrats — roughly 40% of the Democratic caucus — and no Republican has signed on, in a House where Republicans hold 223 of 440 seats and control every committee chairmanship and the floor calendar.

industries.industry: Retail, food service, and hospitality employers
industries.note: These industries employ the most hourly, part-time, and tipped workers without paid vacation, so they bear the largest new payroll cost — up to 80 paid hours per employee per year. What costs them is exactly what workers gain: paid time off they currently work without.

The bill covers any employer with even one employee, with no small-business exemption, so the smallest firms face the same accrual, recordkeeping, notice, and payout obligations as large chains, with the least capacity to absorb them.

Unions gain a new enforcement route: members can use their contract's grievance and arbitration process to enforce bargained leave provisions, and the federal floor cannot override stronger union contracts.

The bill sweeps in federal agencies, state employees, congressional offices, the GAO, and the Library of Congress, each with its own enforcement path — a rare federal mandate that applies to the government as an employer, not just private business.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in five committees with no hearings scheduled, no Republican cosponsors, and a Republican majority controlling both committee agendas and the floor calendar. The most likely outcome, based on how bills at this stage typically fare, is that it never advances and expires when the Congress ends on January 3, 2027; a remote path would be revival through a larger labor or spending package, or reintroduction in a future Congress.
